caption:
A Christmas market in Cornwall, England, was advertised with AI images of glowing stalls, garlands and an ice rink.
Visitors found a mostly empty hall with buckets catching water from a leak.
The organizer has now canceled and refunded every booking.

Would you still trust an event ad that was made with AI?

threads_text: A Christmas market in Cornwall sold itself with AI pictures of lights, garlands and an ice rink. People showed up to a mostly empty hall with buckets catching a roof leak, and now every booking is canceled. Should AI images in event ads come with a label?

paragraphs.text: A Christmas market in Cornwall, England, has canceled every booking after shoppers and traders said the event looked nothing like the AI-generated images used to promote it. The Kernow Christmas Market in Pool opened on November 20, 2026, according to a Mirror report republished by AOL on November 25.

The market was billed as an add-on to Cornwall's Winter Wonderland attraction and was set to run every Saturday and Sunday until Christmas Eve, Capital Digest reported. It was held at the Pool Market hall.

The promotional images showed rows of stalls under strings of lights, garlands and wreaths, an ice rink outside, and a wooden lodge bar with sofa seating, tables, a large screen and a stage, the Mirror reported. Another image showed a decorated book stand. AI Weekly, summarizing BBC reporting, said traders had been told to expect more than 50 stalls and over 2,500 visitors a day.

Visitors described something very different. According to the Mirror, they found a hall that was mostly empty, with five buckets in the middle collecting water from a leak. One visitor, Sammie Retallick, said there were only five stalls and no decorations or lights. Capital Digest reported that photos showed concrete floors, sparse stalls, goods laid out on sheets and a half-decorated tree in what looked like an empty warehouse.

A vendor who paid 30 pounds a day called the situation an absolute shambles and complained that no one would take responsibility, the Mirror reported, citing Cornwall Live. AI Weekly reported that one trader had paid 180 pounds for a pitch. Online, several commenters compared the event to the Willy's Chocolate Experience in Glasgow in February 2024.

Other comments on social media urged the organizers to stop using unrealistic AI images and to pay an artist instead. One local told reporters they had expected trouble as soon as they saw the AI adverts, according to Capital Digest.

Rowlands Attractions, which advertised the event, said it was as disappointed as everyone else that things did not go as planned. It said its agreement was with Pool Market, under which Rowlands advertised the market and booked the stalls while the venue handled the rest. The company said it would cancel and refund all current and future bookings and that the Kernow Christmas Market would take no further bookings for 2026. Traders who want to keep selling must book directly with Pool Market.

According to the Mirror, traders were also offered a free trading space at Cornwall Winter Wonderland. AI Weekly reported, citing the BBC, that the creator of the wider Winter Wonderland attraction, who made the AI images, said they were meant to give a rough idea of the planned experience rather than an exact picture of the venue. Pool Market had not responded to requests for comment at the time of the Mirror report.

Image generators have made it cheap for small organizers to produce polished promotional art, but this case shows how quickly that can backfire when the picture promises far more than the venue delivers. The gap was easy for visitors to document with their own phones, and the backlash ended the event within days of opening.
The case adds to pressure on event organizers to label AI-generated promotional images or to show real photos of a venue, especially in the busy holiday season.
